replacements.instruction: Keep the formal W/(W+L) definition once in Experimental Design, but do not repeat formula notation in captions or other reader-facing locations; make the existing paper CI fail if it is repeated outside the canonical definition.
replacements.before: \caption{Cross-family judge robustness using \modelCross. Within each selected contrast, W/L/T counts are summed over benchmarks before computing $W/(W+L)$; all three contrasts favor our system, but 3 of 9 benchmark-level comparisons reverse relative to the primary judge and many outcomes are ties. Commit is the fraction of eligible pairs with a non-tied cross-family outcome; Agreement is the fraction whose order-consistent outcome matches the primary judge.}
replacements.after: \caption{Cross-family judge robustness using \modelCross. Within each selected contrast, wins, losses, and ties are summed over benchmarks before computing the win rate; all three contrasts favor our system, but 3 of 9 benchmark-level comparisons reverse relative to the primary judge and many outcomes are ties. Commit is the fraction of eligible pairs with a non-tied cross-family outcome; Agreement is the fraction whose order-consistent outcome matches the primary judge.}

replacements.instruction: Rewrite the Table 7 caption so it first states what the table reports, then gives the process-path comparison, aggregation scope, and observational qualification; do not repeat the win-rate formula here.
replacements.before: \caption{Planning--drafting--reviewing and other-path runs have similar win rates against \condFixedOrder\ and \condSingleWriter. Rates use wins/losses summed across benchmarks and three runs for each path group and comparison; the split is observational, not causal.}
replacements.after: \caption{Win rates for our system against \condFixedOrder\ and \condSingleWriter, grouped by observed process path. Planning--drafting--reviewing and other-path runs show similar rates. Rates aggregate wins and losses across benchmarks and three generation runs within each path group and comparison; the split is observational, not causal.}
